analysis.one_liner: Bans members of Congress and their spouses from trading individual stocks while in office.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Administration Committee on May 5, 2025, and has sat there ever since with zero cosponsors, no hearing, and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change federal ethics law to bar sitting members of Congress and their spouses from buying, selling, or holding individual stocks, stock options, commodities, or similar investments. Members could keep diversified mutual funds, index funds, federal Thrift Savings Plan accounts, and Treasury bonds, or could place assets in a qualified blind trust. Violations would carry a civil fine. The rules would not take effect until the start of the next Congress, in 2027.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans who want lawmakers deciding laws that move markets without personally betting on the outcomes. It would also protect the integrity of legislation affecting specific companies, since members could no longer hold shares in the firms their committees regulate. Members and spouses whose only investments are diversified funds or federal retirement accounts lose nothing.

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits members of Congress and their spouses from holding, purchasing, or selling any 'covered financial instrument' — individual securities, security futures, commodities, and derivative positions such as options — during the member's term of service [S2].
It closes the loophole Congress has wrestled with since the STOCK Act of 2012, which required disclosure of trades but never banned them, by making the trading itself off-limits [S2].
It would take effect on the first day of the 120th Congress (January 2027), giving current members a runway before the rules bind [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Sitting members of Congress and their spouses, who would have to give up personal stock and commodity trading or park those assets in a blind trust. Members holding individual stocks would either sell before taking office or be barred from selling during their term.
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress and their spouses

drawbacks.text: Members who owned individual stocks before taking office may keep holding them; the ban on 'holding' does not apply to instruments owned immediately preceding the member's term, so legacy holdings remain in place [S2].
Enforcement is weak: violations carry only a civil fine under the existing penalty structure in the same chapter of law, and no independent enforcement mechanism is created [S2].
The rules do not bind anyone until the first day of the 120th Congress, so members trading today would face no restriction for the remainder of this term [S2].
Well-managed blind trusts and diversified funds remain fully permitted, so the bill does not touch most members' actual retirement wealth — only direct market trading [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but narrow: it removes direct personal stock trading by lawmakers without touching diversified funds or retirement accounts, so the cost to members is limited to giving up direct market bets. The design flaws — grandfathered holdings, modest fines, and a 2027 start date — dilute it, but as a first binding prohibition on congressional stock trading it is a genuine, if partial, fix. Its fatal problem so far is not the design but the absence of any action on it.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Administration Committee on the day it was introduced and has had no hearing, no markup, and no vote since.

narrative.text: Representative Bresnahan introduced the bill on May 5, 2025 [S1,S4].
It was referred to the Committee on House Administration the same day, its only action to date [S4].
No other member has signed on as a cosponsor [S3].

The bill would amend title 5 of the U.S. Code to bar members and spouses from holding, buying, or selling individual stocks, options, commodities, and similar instruments during their terms, with exceptions for diversified funds, the Thrift Savings Plan, Treasury securities, and qualified blind trusts [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill has gone nowhere, current members of Congress keep their existing ability to trade individual stocks while in office; no member has yet had to change behavior.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Members who trade stocks in office

for.name: Rep. Robert P. Bresnahan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on May 5, 2025; it has drawn no cosponsors from either party since [S1,S3,S4].

against.name: Rep. Bryan Steil
against.role: Chair, House Committee on House Administration
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee the bill was referred to, has not scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving the bill without a path to the floor.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Have not brought a stock-trading ban to the House floor this Congress, despite multiple member proposals.

sides.party_line_note: No vote has occurred and the bill has zero cosponsors, so the record shows only a lone Republican sponsor and no measurable support from either party.

industries.industry: Members of Congress and their spouses
industries.note: The bill would bar them from buying, selling, or holding individual stocks, options, and commodities while in office, and fine violators. Members currently may trade so long as they disclose, so this is the concentrated interest the bill targets directly [S2].

The bill excludes diversified mutual funds, ETFs, the Thrift Savings Plan, and Treasury securities from the ban, so most mainstream investment vehicles are untouched; only direct individual-security trading by lawmakers ends. No brokerage or fund industry group is named in the record as affected.

analysis.trajectory: Bills banning congressional stock trading have been introduced repeatedly in recent Congresses, drawn attention and occasional committee hearings, but none has reached a floor vote. With zero cosponsors and a committee chair who controls the calendar taking no action, the realistic path is that this bill sits in committee until the 119th Congress ends in January 2027. If leadership ever embraced it, the text already delays compliance until 2027 anyway.
